Spooling up a coal fired power plant is not as easy as turning a switch.

The first step is simply providing the coal to the furnace for firing. Coal plants have large areas of land dedicated to simply feeding the beast. Assuming that we simply use it infrequently, we have to pay to keep someone constantly on the ready and maintain the (now) unused conveyors.

Then we have the challenge of reheating a now cool furnace. Coal can burn upwards of 3500 degrees F but you can't suddenly heat to that high; that takes either time or energy to preheat.

Then you finally have the coal burning it starts to heat up the water in the boiler. The water either a) is cooled well below boil temp (same issue as with the furnace, just now we have a larger mass to heat that doesn't produce it's own heat) or b) we use energy to maintain it at a higher temperature.

Once we finally have a hot fire heating boiling water, at least the turbines will start to produce right away. That is if they are smaller and use ball or roller bearings (that are properly maintained). If not, it uses hydrodynamic bearings which require time and speed to properly rotate the shaft, thus killing momentum provided by the steam.

You could make smaller power plants, but then the costs rise SHARPLY due to higher speeds and therefore greater wear.

I will submit that smaller plants, though plagued by higher maintenance costs, would be able to supplement wind or solar if needed. The better practice would be to use oil or gas but that also opens it's own can of worms but far fewer than coal in this scenario.

Third, Texas has a unique market structure. It’s complicated, but ERCOT has set up the grid in such a way that it acquires a large amount of power through continuous auctions. Every five minutes, power generators in the state electronically bid into ERCOT’s real-time market, offering to provide chunks of energy at particular prices. ERCOT fills the open needs by selecting the bids that are cheapest and that make the most sense from a grid-management perspective—i.e., the power is being fed into the grid at points where the distribution and transmission systems can handle it. Every 15 minutes, the bids settle—at the highest price paid for electricity accepted in the round. So if 100 MW of electricity are needed, and some producers offer 60 MW at $50 per megawatt-hour, some offer 30 MW at $80 per megawatt-hour, and others offer 40 MW at $100 per megawatt-hour, all the bidders will receive the highest price of $100. (Note: The price ERCOT pays is the wholesale generation charge.)

After midnight on Sunday, the combination of these three factors pushed the real-time price of electricity lower. Demand fell—at 4 a.m., the amount of electricity needed in the state was about 45 percent lower than the evening peak. At 3 a.m., wind was supplying about 30 percent of the state’s electricity, as this daily wind integration report shows. And because the state is an electricity island, all the power produced by the state’s wind farms could only be sold to ERCOT, not grids elsewhere in the country.

That gave wind-farm owners a great incentive to lower their prices.
